Revised assessment incorporating literature: The statement is hawkish in response to elevated, largely supply-driven inflation. The FOMC’s emphasis on expectations and commitment to 2 percent aligns with inflation-forecast targeting frameworks (Svensson and Woodford, 2005), and its operating-tool mix (IOER and ON RRP) reflects modern implementation principles for rate control (Goodfriend, 2002). The inflation surge is consistent with a New Keynesian Phillips Curve view in which cost-push shocks (pandemic disruptions, China lockdowns) and energy price shocks from the Russia–Ukraine war raise marginal costs and depress activity, a classic stagflationary configuration where oil shocks weigh on growth. Recent “inflation-at-risk” evidence points to upside-skewed inflation outcomes when supply shocks and constraints dominate, justifying front-loaded policy tightening and balance-sheet reduction. While such tightening should help anchor expectations and reduce long-run disinflation costs (credibility channel), near-term growth risks rise as financial conditions tighten. Netting these, the tone remains slightly negative, but less so than a purely risk-focused read.
